video_title: We Tested Ten SUVs, Which One's the Best?
author: @cd7856
comment:
Nicely produced, but the reviews seem overly focused on infotainment, not on price, quality, safety features or crash test ratings.

I like the Tuscon. I actually rented one for a week this year.  Fuel economy, price, performance, features, infotainment, yada-yada, all pretty good.  But, the  trim level I had didn't have some current safety features and the Tucson's IIHS crash test ratings are not quite as good as others.   So,  it is a no for us.

The Sorento isn't bad.  Nice, quiet, fuel efficient, good infotainment, nice design, fuel efficient, good ride...   I just cannot stand the climate control being merged with other stuff.  Very hard to use.  Kind of a deal breaker.   Also, the car also feels a bit small.  So, not buying it.     But,  safety features are great.  Haven't checked out the crash ratings.    

The Rav4...  Two major complaints 1) A car is for driving. The thing is so lethargic.  You guys are totally right -- It is like a bigger Prius!     How can you enjoy driving it?  I mean, I owned a Prius and it was great, but so unresponsive.    I would be afraid to have my wife pull onto a busy road driving this thing.  A definite no!      2) The inside is small.   The front feels more likea pod/cockpit than an open space and the rear seats are small.   If you're above 6ft, good luck....     I test drove a couple Rav4s.   The rest of what the guys say is true, but man,... 

The CR-V is pretty good unless you are into towing.    Main concern would be the engine issues experienced by some model years.   Fortunately some dealerships offer a lifetime powertrain warranty to cover this concern.    Also, the rear crash test rating is  POOR through MY 2025.  Yes, "POOR", as in "very bad"....  Not sure if that is fixed for MY2026, but something to consider/research if you frequently carry rear passengers.  

Final point, not sure why you guys are pushing the hybrids.  For most of these, you wont' make your hybrid upcharge in fuel savings until you reach 150k miles or more.   That does not even consider the interest you would have earned on the $5000 or so paid for a hybrid.   With modes investment success, you'd double your money every 10 years or so.   That means, you'd have to drive roughly 300,000 miles to get your money back.    Who drives 30,000 miles a year, anyway?.....  Rough math i know.... and some prefer to safe the evironment with batteries instead of coal, but from a financial point of view, hybrids makes little or no sense.

author: @richardausten5295
comment: Historically, Toyota and Honda have been the most reliable cars. But it depends on which models and times have changed. First-year models of a new generation score lower, and Toyota, in particular, have put out a slew of new cars. So their reliability dropped. Subaru ranked number one in December 2024 as the most reliable car brand overall - BMW was 2nd or 3rd, uncharacteristically for a German brand. But reliability is part of the equation - the dealer experience also matters. Reviewers at Savagegeese note the generally awful dealer experience with both Korean brands. You get a 10-year warranty that they won't honour - so what good is that? They have also had millions of 4-cylinder cars recalled for catching fire. Toyota has had all kinds of problems over the last couple of years. The Car Care Nut channel is terrific because he goes over all the cars with a fine-tooth comb, detailing all the problems from a mechanic's perspective, looking at all of the engine parts, the shocks, the transmission, and points out all the weak spots. He recently gave glowing takes on the Honda Passport and Hyundai Palisade. But he still points out their weak spots, like the VCM in the Passport and that they use a timing belt. He notes how difficult things will be to fix (which means more expensive) down the road. The dealer experience is critical - Kia Hynundai may be totally fine in your city and rubbish in another, ditto Honda or Toyota, etc. All cars eventually break down, so you want to be sure the dealer is going to do right by you.  Sometimes it may make more sense to choose the 3rd most reliable car if you know the dealer is rock solid over the 1st most reliable car when the dealership has a reputation of blaming you and not doing the repairs. While I have never owned Lexus - I generally hear the service is absolutely first rate.

- Used 2008 V6 Sport Rav4.  Had it for 5 years after I bought it used and put about 70k km.  No problems other than failing sunroof.  In the end the back seat was just too uncomfortable (seats too low) as the kids got bigger.

I had a 22 Mazda3 sedan in the premium plus turbo trim and there were a lot of things I loved about it. What made me trade it in for my 25 Civic Hybrid ST was the fuel efficiency, ride quality, and interior/cargo space. 

The Mazda felt luxurious on the inside, until you hit even slightly rough roads. I can still feel the shakes on the highway that night. What drove me up the wall was it's less than reported MPG. With that turbo, I was happy to see 24mpg combined, but most of the time I got 21. Combine that with a small tank meant regular fuel ups every 1 to 1.5 weeks. 

The Civic, especially in the hatchback option, checked all the boxes I needed. Spacious, fun to drive, speedy, and fuel efficient. What do I miss on the Mazda? The 360 camera, lumbar support, and honestly, the infotainment. I love that dial. But it wasn't worth the rough ride and constant fuel ups on what is supposed to be a commuter compact, not a sports car.

comment:
This is a great video with wonderful information, but the AI "narrator" is off on some things (IN-teh-gra - nope In-TEH-gra). I also wouldn't call an I-4 engine in such surplatives, unless the car really deserves it (e.g., close to 400hp, 350 lb/ft). the turbocharged inline 4 is in most small cars - and, sadly more in mid-sized cars.

The Audi RS series is interesting: regardless of the model (RS3, RS4, RS5, RS7...) they all have comparable numbers. 0-60? Around 3.5 seconds (thanks to amazing engines mostly shipped from the Porsche factory in Stuttgart and the rally-tried Quattro AWD). Top Speed? About 175mph. comment: I'm one of those that believe a muscle car is basically an American car that has a high horsepower high torque V8 under the hood. -Sportscar: A car whose primary focus is on handling, braking and enjoyable driving dynamics. Typcially affordable by of-age middle class households. Almost exclusively limited to two useful seats. Offers straight line performance above most cars in lower tiers but there are edge cases where this is not the case. EG: Corvette, 911, Jag F type, 370Z 

-GT Car: A sporty car with significant luggage capacity. Focus is less on outright dynamics, prioritizing enough comfort to make long drives pleasant. Often trades cornering/braking performance for highway-usable power. More expensive than muscle and pony cars which have similar characteristics. EG: //M cars, AMG cars, Aston Martins

-Sports luxury: Lower-priced GT cars which attempt to mimic the luxurious and sporting attributes of GT cars while typically offering less outright power. EG: Inifiniti G37, Lexus RC350, 228I Msport, Audi S3

-Muscle Car: The inverse of a sports car, prioritizing straight-line speed over cornering ability. Typically coupes built on full-size frames with four usable seats. Considerably more affordable than GT cars, but generally worse handling characteristics and quality. US/AUS manufacturers. Almost exclusively V8 powered. EG: Challenger, Charger, Chevy SS, Holden Monaro.

-Pony Car: Compact affordable coupes patterned after the ford mustang model, targeted to young adults. Prioritizes fun over other attributes. Typcically fall on the spectrum between Sports, GT and Muscle cars. EG: Ford Mustang, Chevy Camaro, Genesis Coupe

-Rally-like cars: Compact four wheel drive performance cars which specialize in all weather and road condition performance. Patterned after the Subaru WRX and Mitsubishi Lancer Evolution. Typically powered by turbocharged four cylinder engines. EG: WRX, EVO 

-Roadster: Sporty two-seater convertibles prioritizing driving fun and light weight over all other factors. Patterned after British compact sporty convertibles. EG: Mazda MX5

-Hot Hatch: Compact and highly affordable performance cars. Typically front wheel drive with four cylinder powerplants which may be turbocharged. 3 or 5 doors.

The C6 was such an improvement, and honestly, at current prices, no excuse not to own one if you want to feel what a V8 American sports car is like. comment:
In Canada, I'd buy either of the two Americans if available for 50k Canadian dollars. But I live in the UK, and for that money it would be a choice between a regular Mustang GT, F-Type V6 S, base 981 Cayman, and a 997.1 911. For me, it would be between the F-Type and the 911. If I wanted an auto it would be the F-Type -- although you can get a manual F-Type for the money -- and if I wanted a manual it would be the 911.

Neither of the two Americans is available in right-hand drive, so would rule them out for most people in the UK, including myself. And neither can be had for anywhere near CAD50k. You also couldn't get a 4C or an i8 for that money in the UK. And you'd also be 'lucky' to get a high mileage V8 F-Type for the money.

The F-Type is good value to buy but they have proven quite needy and aren't in any way cheap to own or maintain. Most petrolheads in the UK would opt for a base 981 Cayman.

IMO, the main downside of the F-Type is what most people think is one of its most compelling features, ie, the engines. For me, the artificially engineered pops and bangs are annoying to live with, and the engines are all poorly designed, which isn't what you want in the longer term. 

I suspect the C7 Corvette will always be desirable, not least for its relative simplicity, and the GT350 will always be desirable simply because of its special engine. Both a good-looking cars, too.

The i8's drivetrain is also something you're not going to want in the longer term. comment:
Two and a half years ago, I was literally the target audience for this video. I was looking for a 2-door sports car and had a budget of $50-60k. I literally had on my short list three of the five cars you guys tested: the C7 Vette, the F-Type R, and the GT350. Here's why I passed on each one of them.

1) The C7 was just "too sporty" for me. It was too low to the ground, had too tight of a cockpit, and didn't have a dedicated trunk. I wanted more of a "grand touring" car, and less of a true "sports" car.
2) The F-Type R wasn't available with a manual transmission. That was a huge buzzkill. A manual was Priority 1 while shopping for my next car. Otherwise, it looked amazing, sounded amazing, and had a very comfortable cockpit. No separate trunk, but I was so smitten with its looks that I didn't care. Jaguar long-term reliability was also a concern however.
3) I was REALLY close to getting a GT350. Having owned a 2015 GT in the past, I was partial to the Mustang. However,  I would only have bought a 2019 or 2020 model due to the changes Ford made to the Voodoo engine and oil system after 2018. Unfortunately, every GT350 from those two model years I found within a few hundred miles of me with less than 10k miles also had an asking price north of $65k and even $70k. I could have easily bought a 2016 or 2017, but worried so much about the engine issues that I couldn't pull the trigger.

So after all that, I eventually ended up buying a 2022 Mustang Mach 1. It had just 700 miles on it during my test drive, so I saved a bundle over buying new. It had the reliability and sound of the Coyote V8, and the buttery-smooth Tremec transmission from the Shelby. Add in the digital gauge cluster, rev-matching, and all the parts from the GT350 and GT500, and it was the perfect car for me in the end. I paid $57k for it (MSRP was $63k), and after two years and 15,000 miles later, I could still sell it for around $50k today no problem. Sure, the GT350 has the Voodoo engine and you get to be part of the "Shelby club" and all that, but I love every minute I spend behind the wheel of the Mach 1. No regrets whatsoever.

author: @CentaXBerlin2
comment:
Wow! I really appreciate your reviews and your views on cars. This one hits so close to home, because a few months ago I bought a 2013 F-Type V8 S convertible in Salsa Red for kind of the same reasons. I wanted the most hardcore RWD version; the V8 R convertible is incredible rare, which was too much of a premium (and actually hard to find) on the used market. Why a convertible? Because you get 200% more sound and involvement. The F-Type was a classical "Hero Car". When Tata bought JLR, they needed to make a statement. So they finally build a proper sports car and dared to name it the E-Type successor. The F-Types objective was not to boost revenue, but to build the company image. No expenses spared, probably. 

I wanted a V8 for many years. Looked at W213 C63s first, they sell for around ~40k€. Insurance kills you however, and they will continue to depreciate as there are a lot. One day it clicked; I don't need practicality now, I can trade the practicability for something way more unique. 

I don't think the F-Type will continue to depreciate. I rather think the contrary. The exhaust is crazy; mine never had a software update, tuning down the pops and bangs. It is registered to 112dB noise level, stock. There is hardly anything louder, as during this time, there was a loophole using valved exhaust systems. The RWD is quite rare. There is no need for more power, it can hardly lay it down in 2nd gear, full traction is only in 3rd - but if it's just slightly wet or slippery, sometimes the rear will slightly slide at 120+km/h. It's something so extreme, which makes it so entertaining and challenging also in the long-term. Sure the AWD is faster, but powersliding every corner and the ability to rebalance in each corner with the instantaneous throttle response is just incredible fun. I can't stay composed in this car, I still laugh manic exactly like you every time I drive it.

But all of that is only when you push it. You can deflate the seats side cushions, put it in D, disengage Dynamic Mode - and it has a fully switched personality. It's relaxing and comfortable, a cruiser that you could daily drive. With retrofitted Android Auto I miss nothing in it.

The cars it was compared against back in the day are for sure better sports cars or better cars overall, but depreciation is your friend. I would not prefer the Vantage V8 to the F-Type; the old Vantage actually has a Jaguar AJ37 non-supercharged V8 and many interior parts from my prior 2006 Volvo C30. Sure it's a nice car that will age well and looks great, but I think the Jaguar gives the better package with the worse badge. I don't care, there is not a single car I would trade my F-Type for.

Owning the F-Type, this car is soo much more than I hoped for. Not just the engine, response, sounds, but also the luxury, refinement, handling, looks. I actually think the V6S is even more bang-for-your-buck, you can get one starting at ~33k€ in germany; you still get thrilling sound, it's just not quite as mental as the V8.

comment:
My order is: 

No #4 Lexus
No #3 Audi
No #2 & No #1 Mercedes and BMW <-- a tie

No #4 Lexus --> Because it has the least amount of technology in it. Mainly in the infotainment system and also engine. Low resolution, small screen, low CPU, lower quality materials (plastic & leather), worse gearbox and the MOST EXPENSIVE of the 4. That is a big show stopper because if it's 5.000 pounds more expensive. It should deliver. It doesn't. I won't pay 5000 extra just to be unique and not go for 'german', right? 

No #3 Audi --> Very well build, I would say that there is almost no difference between the 3 (Audi, Merc & BMW) in the build quality of the materials (leather and plastics). Audi has that DSG which sometimes has lag and also that weight distribution problem being so damn heavy in the front. The Google contract saved them because the Audi infotainment system sucked BIG TIME before. Now, with Google on your map and on your gauges it's a big step forward. Still a very good car but I have to agree with Mat on the design. From my point of view it looks like a Ford Mondeo in the front. 

No#2 & No#1 A tie --> from the technological point of view it's a tie, although I love the BMW's gearbox and also the iDrive is above the Merc's. But, I agree with the looks of the Mercedes (exterior and interior) are much nicer than the BMW's. Both cars have an exceptional driving dynamics at high speeds and also in corners. I would choose the BMW but it's just a matter of taste. And forget about the all wheel drive at all of these cars. They are meant to be driven raw, without the 'handicap' of 4x4. In this day and age, all the electronic systems on board will keep you on the road even on snow and ice (of course if you are a responsible driver). The 4x4 system will make the car heavier, ruin the weight distribution and most important will ruin the sensation of the cars torque pressing you down on the seat when you put your foot down. Again, just a matter of taste also but I feel like people are buying the 4x4 systems just to be safe because the haven't driven a RWD car before and ... they are afraid. Usually first bimmer owners go for the 4x4 because 15 years ago RWD sucked. Well ... technology evolved you know ... a lot. 

Good review Mat! Keep up the good work!

comment: I'm 21 and picked up my C Class Coupe 4 months ago, my first Mercedes, so hopefully I can offer a bit of owner experience! First of all, opinions on the looks are just that........opinions. I agree, I prefer to look at the car from the front because the diamond grille and chrome splitter really sets it off, but then I like the back because it's clearly been based off the S Class, a car waaaay out of my price range and a lot of others too. Then there's the interior, the best part of the car for me. Mine is the obsidian black metallic exterior, with the beige/cream artico leather interior, complete with the same black ash wood console in the video which, in my opinion (again, entirely subjective), is the best interior in its class at the moment. Its hard to believe that such an interior is available in a car in this price range, of which mine was just above £42000 as has a multitude of options. It's the C250d with the 2.1 diesel and 9 speed auto (of which is a fantastic gearbox), I'm returning on average 55mpg at the moment after 2500 miles. My one hate about the car though? How unrefined the diesel engine sounds. Going along its absolutely fine and you can't tell you sound like you're driving a tractor haha! It's when you are at idle or come to a stop that it's bad. But then the cabin is so quiet that you do well to hear anything outside of it! Acceleration? It isn't slow by any means, a multitude of torque helps with that and in the real world you'd do well to tell the difference between any of the cars tested. Honestly, I was surprised at how well it handles corners, especially in Sport but push a bit more and you start to understeer a bit; characteristics of a heavy Mercedes I would have thought!
